explanation: Pistachios and poison ivy are in the family too. Cashew shells and mango skin contain irritants related to poison ivy's, which is why cashews are sold shelled.

claims.text: The cashew (Anacardium occidentale) and the mango (Mangifera indica) both belong to the family Anacardiaceae.
The almond (Rosaceae), walnut (Juglandaceae) and coconut (Arecaceae) belong to other plant families than the cashew.
The pistachio and poison ivy also belong to the family Anacardiaceae.
Cashew shells and mango skin contain irritant compounds related to urushiol, the irritant in poison ivy.
Cashews are sold shelled because their shells contain caustic irritants.

evidence.restatement: Almond is in the rose family (Rosaceae), walnut in Juglandaceae and coconut in the palm family (Arecaceae).
Pistachio and poison ivy are also in Anacardiaceae.
Cashew shells hold caustic anacardic acids and cardol, and mango skin holds urushiol-like resorcinols, relatives of poison ivy's urushiol.
Cashews are sold shelled because the shell's caustic oil has to be removed in processing.
Cashew (Anacardium) and mango (Mangifera) are both in Anacardiaceae, the sumac family.

evidence.restatement: Almond is Rosaceae, walnut Juglandaceae and coconut Arecaceae.
Pistachio (Pistacia) and poison ivy (Toxicodendron) are in Anacardiaceae.
Cashew nut-shell liquid and mango peel and sap contain alkylphenols and resorcinols chemically related to urushiol and can cause the same contact rash.
Cashews in the shell are not sold because the shell holds a caustic oil; the nuts are removed and heat-treated first.
